data.title: Data center spending to more than double to $2.1 trillion by 2028, BofA says
data.description:
(Corrects to add attribution in headline)

Oct 23 (Reuters) - Global data center spending is expected to hit $1 trillion in 2026 and more than double to $2.1 trillion by 2028, BofA Global Research estimated in a note on Friday, driven by growing demand for and development of AI services.

Data center spending has been a fast-growing source of revenue for industrial firms that make generators, construction equipment, switchgears and chillers.

Here are the details

-- The data center market, worth $275 billion in 2022, could reach $2.93 trillion by 2030, BofA said

-- AI is seen driving the expansion, which the brokerage says will fuel a 37% market-wide CAGR from 2025 to 2030, the brokerage said

-- Chipmakers and server developers have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI-driven data center buildout, particularly in the US

-- BofA put data center construction costs at $49 million per megawatt, with IT-related expenses making up 78% of total spend

-- Neoclouds, or AI-focused data centers, cost about $57 million per megawatt but benefit from lower space requirements than traditional counterparts

-- The brokerage estimates servers are the costliest component at $31.4 million per megawatt, and networking the second-largest at $4.8 million per megawatt

-- Most other functions - switchgear, power distribution, generators, backup power, chillers and cooling - cost between $100,000 to $1.1 million per megawatt

(Reporting by Nandan Mandayam in Bengaluru; Editing by Tasim Zahid)

data.title: Taiwan's Stock Pickers Are Walking Out to Bet Their Own Money
data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly On Wall Street News Commentary - Taiwan's benchmark stock index was up 62% this year, the best showing of any major equity gauge in the world, when Bloomberg reported on Oct. 16 that some of the island's professional fund managers and analysts are quitting their jobs to invest their own money. Strict rules keep them from trading the very stocks they pick for clients, and in a year when about one in ten stocks in the index has more than doubled, some have decided the trade-off is no longer worth it. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited ( TSM ) [TSMC] , ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. ( ASX ) [ASE] , United Microelectronics Corporation ( UMC ) [UMC] , iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF , The Taiwan Fund, Inc. ( TWN ) .

Watching From Behind the Locker

Taiwan does not ban personal investing outright, but its asset-management code of conduct bars staff from trading a locally listed stock or a linked derivative within seven business days before or after their firm's funds trade it, which in practice rules out personal stock-picking. Fund managers must also lock away their phones, laptops and smartwatches each morning until the market closes at 1:30 p.m. The phone rule was formalized in 2024 to deter insider trading, the Taipei Times reported in July, after six former fund managers from four firms were indicted for front-running trades through the accounts of relatives and friends.

Ken Tsai, 40, a fund manager who until July worked at a large Taiwanese asset manager that Bloomberg did not name, told Bloomberg he made a Taiwanese maker of AI-server data-transfer components his fund's largest holding in 2024. The stock rose more than fivefold in 2025 and about sixfold again this year, but he owned none of it personally. "It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation," he said. He now works at a private investment firm in Taipei, which was also not named. Pay adds to the pull: Taiwan portfolio managers earn roughly US$124,000 to US$311,000 a year, well below Hong Kong base salaries, according to Bloomberg, citing headhunters and recruitment-firm data.

The private shops they are joining sit outside those rules. They register as private companies with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and do not need asset-management licenses from the Financial Supervisory Commission because they do not raise public money. Brokers told Bloomberg some of them now generate more than NT$10 billion in monthly trading volume, rivaling mid-sized asset managers.

The Rally Behind the Exits

Much of the rally traces back to the AI hardware supply chain. TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (US$46.7 billion) on Oct. 15, up 50.9% from a year earlier, while net income jumped 68.7% and gross margin reached 66.4%. It guided fourth-quarter revenue from US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion.

Chip packaging and testing has ridden the same wave. ASE Technology ( ASX ) reported September net revenue of NT$88.1 billion, up 45.5% from a year earlier, and third-quarter revenue of NT$244.2 billion, up 44.8%.

Mature-node foundry UMC reported August sales up 30.71% from a year earlier, lifting year-to-date sales 14.66%. In its second-quarter report, the company guided for capacity utilization above 90% in the third quarter and said revenue from its 22/28nm business continues to set record highs.

CONTINUED... Read more market coverage at: flyonwallstreet.com

A Talent Squeeze, Not a Stampede

The numbers point to churn more than an exodus. Fewer than half of Taiwan's 20 largest local equity mutual funds have kept the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data site MoneyDJ, and Bloomberg reported that applications for junior roles at some international firms have roughly halved this year. Yet the FSC said the industry's registered headcount actually rose to 4,729 in September from 4,581 at the end of 2025. Firms are responding: the largest foreign asset manager in Taiwan is offering cross-market analyst roles and office rotations to keep staff.

Regulators are paying attention. The FSC said on Oct. 15 it is gathering information and plans to review the rules, balancing market development against conflicts of interest and investor protection. One asset-management executive told Bloomberg there is no easy solution for now.

The Case for the Pros

At least one professionally managed fund has kept pace. The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ), a closed-end fund listed in New York, reported a 47.36% total return for its fiscal quarter ended May 31, against 26.12% for the TAIEX Total Return Index over the same period, with net asset value of US$116.90 a share at the end of that quarter.

Investors who prefer to own the whole market can use the iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF, which holds about US$11.9 billion in assets.

Last week was a reminder of how quickly the math can change. The TAIEX fell 4.6%, its first weekly decline in five weeks, as a technology selloff spread and TSMC CEO C.C. Wei warned of macroeconomic uncertainty and weak consumer demand, according to Trading Economics. In New York, TSMC's shares fell 8.98% from the Oct. 9 close to $412.61 on Oct. 16, ASE dropped 14.86% to $39.53, UMC slid 13.68% to $19.82, the iShares fund lost 7.04% to $106.26 and The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ) declined 8.78% to $94.18, according to Stock Analysis data. For the managers who just traded a salary for their own account, those swings now land on them.

data.title: EXPLAINER-What is going on with SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine?
data.description:
(Updates earlier factbox with more information about use in Ukraine)

WASHINGTON/KYIV, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine's military has been hit this month by restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system. Its receivers stopped functioning when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones, jeopardising some combat and air defence missions.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that SpaceX boss Elon Musk had restored services, although he has denied having spoken to Musk personally about it. But Ukrainian defence and military sources told Reuters on Friday that speed restrictions on Starshield remained in place.

HOW DOES UKRAINE USE STARLINK AND STARSHIELD?

Ukraine's military uses both Starlink for communications and Starshield for specialised military purposes.

The satellite internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival with the capabilities of SpaceX's products.

Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine.But the recent limitation cuts them off when moving faster than 160 kilometres per hour (100 mph).

Ukrainian officials say that hinders drones used for strikes on Russian targets deep inside Ukraine and in some high-speed interceptors to counter Russian drone attacks.

Ukraine's use of Starshield-enabled mid-range attack drones has been a major factor this year in turning the tide on the battlefield, allowing remote pilots to guide drones striking moving targets such as Russian supply trucks and trains.

And fast-moving interceptor drones are one of Ukraine's few systems to protect its cities from one of Russia's own major innovations of recent months: jet-engine-powered attack drones, now used in strikes each night.

WHO GAVE THE ORDER TO RESTRICT IT?

Neither Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for curtailing Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine, and both have said publicly such decisions could only have been taken by the other.

Reuters reported last week that the order to limit the system came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The Wall Street Journal, however, reported on Wednesday, citing sources, that the throttling had been ordered personally by Musk.

After the limitations became public, Musk said that Starshield was owned and controlled by the US government, and that any limits on its speed or usage were decided by the US military and ultimatelyby Trump. He contrasted this with the commercial Starlink system, which he said was not designed or authorised for military use.

Trump has denied being involved in any decision concerning the slowdown. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that ​decisions regarding Ukraine's access to ​Starlink were up to SpaceX and Musk, not the White House.

The restriction comes amid a low point in relations between Kyiv and Washington as Trump seeks to push Kyiv into accepting stronger concessions in a peace deal with Moscow.

Trump has also been pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, although Starshield is not used on drones conducting those attacks as it does not operate over Russian territory.

HOW DOES STARLINK WORK?

Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.

Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.

WHAT IS STARSHIELD?

Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.

While its missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink satellite constellation as their backbone.

In addition to secure communications, SpaceX says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.

The Pentagon, Starshield's largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.

Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.

Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using Starshield services costing five times as much.

(Reporting by Joey Roulette, Cassell Bryan-Low and Max Hunder Editing by Joe Brock and Peter Graff)

data.title: CANADA STOCKS-TSX slips to one-week low as oil, bond yields fuel inflation fears
data.description:
By Anand Gopal R

Oct 23 (Reuters) - Canada's main stock index slipped on Friday to a one-week low, as broad-based losses weighed on the benchmark after rising oil prices and bond yields fueled fears of prolonged inflation and higher-for-longer US interest rates.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index fell 0.83% to 35,673.55 points as of 10:44 a.m. ET, heading for its steepest weekly decline in six weeks, with energy the only sector to gain on Friday, up 2.2%.

* Brent crude prices rose 2.6% to more than a five-month high after escalating hostilities between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia

* Yields in the Canadian benchmark 10-year bond rose more than five basis points to 3.83% after falling for three straight sessions, while yields on the more rate-sensitive 2-year bond rose to 3.34%

* "The mortgages are going to unfortunately impact their (households') ability to spend in other areas along with higher energy costs. It's not necessarily a material risk right now, but it would be a slowdown if that remains the case," said Kevin Headland, co-chief investment strategist at Manulife Investment Management

* Materials sector, including metal miners, fell 1.8% as gold prices slipped, with persistently high oil prices weighing on bullion

* Tech stocks were down 0.8% as selloff in AI-related stocks deepened on the Wall Street

* Heavyweight financials declined 1.7%, while six other sub-sectors also fell more than 1%

* Traders expect the US Federal Reserve to keep rates on hold at its policy meeting next week, with a quarter-point hike priced in for December, according to LSEG data

* In Canada, markets are pricing in a quarter-point Bank of Canada rate hike in its policy meeting next week, according to LSEG data

* Canadian retail sales rose 1.2% in August from July, slightly less than expected

* Telecom operator Rogers Communications reported third-quarter profit above estimates. But, shares fell 1.2%

(Reporting by Anand Gopal and Utkarsh Hathi in Bengaluru; Editing by Tasim Zahid)

data.title: EU ministers vow to tackle 'China Shock 2.0' through talks with Beijing
data.description:
DUBLIN, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The European Union should strike deals with Beijing to curb imports in sectors such as chemicals, machinery and pharmaceuticals, EU ministers said on Friday, as the bloc faces an 'unsustainable' and damaging goods trade deficit with China.

European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic earlier this month agreed with Beijing for the EU to cut imports of hybrid vehicles from China by more than half to address a deficit that has swelled to more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion) a day, and to support Europe's struggling carmakers.

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee told reporters dialogue with China could be a stepping stone "to look to more industries and sectors where we can address that imbalance."

China needs foreign buyers for the flood of relatively cheap state-subsidised goods its own shoppers can't absorb, and the EU is torn between welcoming those imports to ease living costs and keeping them out to rebuild its own factories.

The EU's goods trade deficit swelled to more than €370 billion ($415.07 billion) in 2025 and is on course to break well past €400 billion this year, a situation European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has called "unsustainable".

European industry says the export surge, dubbed China Shock 2.0, is already causing factory closures and job losses, most notably the 100,000 positions set to go at Volkswagen. 

China has said in the past it is not the root cause of the EU's problems, but a partner in solving them. 

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this week there were growing concerns for chemicals and machinery. Lithuania Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said on Friday that pharmaceuticals could also be included.

Ministers did not go into potential short-term measures the EU could take in parallel to discussions with Beijing. 

Greece Deputy Foreign Minister Haris Theoharis said the EU had held talks with China for years without results, but these were now forthcoming.

"We should be continuing to engage in this process, and of course keep all the options open," he said before the meeting of trade ministers.

France's junior minister for trade, Nicolas Forissier, said dialogue was possible now that the EU was speaking as one.  

Chinese authorities "understand when you are clear, when you speak frankly, when you are firm on your positions," he said. 

($1 = 0.8914 euros)

(Reporting by Philip Blenkinsop; editing by Alexandra Hudson)

data.title: FOREX-Euro sinks on French debt worries; yen gains on AI rout
data.description:
(Updated in New York morning time)

* Euro drops on concerns over French unrest, Moody's rating decision awaited

* Japanese yen benefits from safe-haven flow after AI rout

* US dollar index headed for modest weekly loss

By Karen Brettell

Oct 23 (Reuters) - The euro fell on Friday and was on track for a weekly loss against both the US dollar and the yen as a selloff in French government bonds pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone sovereign debt crisis in 2011.

The Japanese yen, meanwhile, was on track for a weekly increase against the greenback as it benefited from safe-haven flows from the selloff in artificial intelligence stocks on Thursday.

The dollar index edged lower on the week, though by less than the euro. Strategists said both currencies came under selling pressure this week, but the euro was hit harder as concerns about growing unrest in France have driven the single currency lower.

France will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday. Meanwhile, the country faces the threat of a rating downgrade by Moody's later on Friday.

"The pressure in the European bond market has eased today, but Moody's review of France's debt rating late today poses a challenge, and although the Macron government has threatened military assistance to quell the social unrest, more activity is likely this weekend," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Global Forex.

The euro was last down 0.12% at $1.12, set to end the week 0.35% lower. It fell more sharply against the yen, touching its lowest level since October 2025 at 175.08 yen on Friday . It was last down 0.31% against the Japanese currency and on track for a weekly decline of 1.3%.

The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.13% to 101.70 and was headed for a weekly loss of 0.10%.

The yen strengthened 0.18% to 156.45 per dollar and was on track for a weekly gain of around 0.9%, its best week since early September.

"The yen has continued to trade at stronger levels at the end of this week, encouraged by more risk-off trading conditions," said Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at MUFG.

CENTRAL BANK POLICY MEETINGS IN FOCUS

Traders turn to next week's policy meetings at the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan. All three are expected to leave rates unchanged, but investors will look for clues on the future path of policy.

Fed funds futures traders trimmed bets on a December hike after Thursday's stock market selloff, though they still see an 81% chance of such a move, according to LSEG data.

Traders see a 66% chance of an ECB hike in December. Investors will scrutinize any hint on the rate outlook after ECB President Christine Lagarde said in late September that a moderate policy response to inflation was appropriate.

Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) data on Friday showed private-sector growth in the euro zone slowed in October to its weakest pace in four months, hurt by a renewed contraction in France.

"The drop brings the PMIs back in line with other growth indicators, in our view, rather than suggesting downside risks from here," Giada Giani, an economist at Citi, said. "France remains a drag, but the rest of the euro area remains resilient."

In Japan, data on Friday showed annual core consumer inflation exceeded the central bank's 2% target in September for the first time in nine months. The reading points to broadening price pressures and strengthens the case for a near-term rate hike.

Traders are pricing in 59% odds of a BOJ hike in December.

(Rporting by Karen Brettell; Additional reporting by Stefano Rebaudo; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria )

data.title: US consumer sentiment near record low ahead of midterm elections
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - US consumer sentiment edged down to near a record low in October as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy on the doorstep of midterm congressional elections centering on affordability issues, a survey showed on Friday.

The University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers said its Consumer Sentiment Index dropped to 48.0 this month from a final reading of 48.1 in September. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the index at 46.3, which had also been the index's preliminary reading for October.

October's reading marked the second-lowest on record after the all-time low of 44.8 set in May, not long after the Iran war began.

"Purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy," said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers. "Sentiment is now 10% below a year ago and 15% less than February, just prior to the Iran conflict."

The survey's measure of consumer expectations for inflation over the next year nudged up to 4.7% from 4.6% in September. Twelve-month inflation expectations have surged from 3.4% in February before the US-Israeli war with Iran started. 

Consumers' expectations for inflation over the next five years rose to 3.5% from 3.4% in September.

Millions of US voters have already cast early ballots in the fast-approaching November 3 midterm election that will determine control of Congress over the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Polls show Republicans are likely to lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as Trump's approval rating in a Reuters/Ipsos poll sits at a record low thanks to the skyrocketing fuel prices unleashed by his decision to attack Iran in late February.

University of Michigan data broken down by political party affiliation showed the weaker sentiment was led by survey respondents self-identified as independents, who comprise a critical bloc of swing voters. Their sentiment score dropped to 42.4 - just above May's record-low 40.6 - from 47.7 in September, while scores for Democrats and Republicans improved.

(Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

data.title: US business activity cools in October; strong demand fueling price pressures
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US business activity slowed modestly in October, though robust demand allowed companies to raise prices for goods and services, a sign that inflation could increase further and remain persistently high in the coming months.

S&P Global said on Friday its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, which tracks the manufacturing and services sectors, slipped to 57.6 this month from a five-year high reading of 58.4 in September. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. Strength in manufacturing was offset by a slight pullback in the vast services sector.

The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing following what is expected to have been a strong performance in the July-September quarter. Economists expect the government's advance gross domestic product report next week to show the economy growing at around a 3.0% annualized rate last quarter, mainly driven by consumer spending and business investment in AI. 

The economy has so far not shown any signs of buckling under the weight of the oil price shock stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran, with savings, generous tax returns in the spring, tariff refunds, a strong stock market performance and corporate profits providing a cushion. Economists warned that the inflation fallout from the drawn-out Middle East conflict was likely to slow consumer spending this quarter.

The survey's measure of new orders received by businesses edged up to 58.2 this month, the highest level since March 2022, from 58.1 in September. The increase was mostly in the services sector, with S&P Global noting "rising domestic demand, boosted partly by precautionary stock building" and growth in exports.

Its gauge of prices for output rose to 59.8, the highest reading since August 2022, from 58.4 in September. Businesses across manufacturing and services sectors raised prices. Delivery performance by suppliers to manufacturers deteriorated further. The survey's measure of suppliers' delivery times dropped to a more than four-year low of 38.1 from 40.9 in September.

SUPPLY BOTTLENECKS INTENSIFYING

"Cost pressures remain a key concern," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers."

Consumer and producer prices increased strongly in September, the government reported this month, raising concerns that inflation was fanning out across the economy. The Federal Reserve in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range. 

Economists expect the US central bank to stand pat at its meeting next week and hike borrowing costs again in December. 

The survey's measure of prices paid by businesses for inputs slipped to a still-high 64.9 from 65.9 in September. Manufacturers, however, faced higher prices this month, with the index still near four-year highs. 

Though overall employment dipped after surging in September, manufacturers boosted headcount. A measure of factory employment increased to the highest level since March 2012, with Williamson saying that companies were seeking "to boost capacity to fulfill stronger customer demand." 

(Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

data.title: Apple's foldable iPhone hits stores with $2,000 price tag and scarce supply
data.description:
By Aditya Soni, Christine Chen and Will Russell

SYDNEY/SHANGHAI/LONDON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Apple's ( AAPL ) first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.

From Singapore and Shanghai to London and Berlin, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days.

Competitors such as Samsung Electronics ( SSNLF ) and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple ( AAPL ) can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones.

It is also an early challenge for Apple's ( AAPL ) new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.

Apple's ( AAPL ) estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary".

Apple ( AAPL ) capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online.

In Sydney, where the first Apple ( AAPL ) store began selling the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT).

"This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a 512GB Duo.

Social media posts showed dozens of customers entering Apple's ( AAPL ) Fifth Avenue store in New York as the iPhone maker's marketing head Greg Joswiak opened the doors. Some posts said people had camped outside the store since as early as 4 a.m. local time (0800 GMT).

In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to six straight quarters of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's ( AAPL ) market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices.

Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi, but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6 a.m. for Apple's ( AAPL ) first foldable.

"I've used Apple ( AAPL ) products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said.

Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models.

Others were resellers.

In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked.

Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain.

"Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said.

MIXED REVIEWS

Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.

But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers.

They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple ( AAPL ) customers.

"It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype - not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple ( AAPL ) commentator John Gruber.

Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone."

In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one.

"I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices."

TOUGH TO FIND

Apple's ( AAPL ) entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC.

IDC expects Apple ( AAPL ) will take 44% of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31% of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.

"Apple ( AAPL ) has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo.

"Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said.

($1 = 1.4257 Australian dollars)

($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

(Reporting by Aditya Soni in Bengaluru, Stephen Nellis in San Francisco, Nicoco Chan in Shanghai, Joyce Zhou in Hong Kong and Christine Chen in Sydney, Matthias Baehr in Berlin, Will Russell and Ben Makori in London, additional reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Will Dunham, Christopher Cushing, Kate Mayberry, Alexander Smith and Leroy Leo)

data.description:
* Spot gold hits lowest level since July

* Brent crude hits more than five-month high

* Fed interest-rate decision, US PCE data due next week

* India gold demand strengthens on lower prices, festive purchases

(Rewrites for US morning session)

By Noel John and Anushree Mukherjee

Oct 23 (Reuters) - Gold recovered from a more than three-month low on Friday, but was headed for a second straight weekly decline as elevated energy prices fuelled inflation concerns and reinforced higher-for-longer rate expectations ahead of next week's US Federal Reserve meeting.

Spot gold edged 0.2% higher to $4,030.67 an ounce by 9:18 a.m. EDT (1318 GMT), after earlier slipping below the $4,000 mark for the first time since mid-July to a session low of $3,986.50. Bullion has lost 3.2% so far this week.

US gold futures for December delivery fell 0.3% to $4,046.40 per ounce.

Brent crude touched a more than five-month high, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies.

"Heightened inflation concerns suggest that major central banks of the world won't be able to ease monetary policies as quickly as they want to. All that's working against the gold and silver market bulls at present," said Jim Wyckoff, a market analyst at American Gold Exchange.

Additionally, "the selloff in the stock market technology sector has prompted margin calls for those stock traders and investors, which is in turn prompting them to sell gold and silver assets," Wyckoff added.

Wall Street's main indexes opened lower as caution prevailed after a sharp selloff in AI-linked stocks.

Meanwhile, traders largely expect the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, although stronger-than-expected US consumer and producer inflation data released last week bolstered the case for tighter monetary policy later this year.

They see a 92% chance of the Fed leaving rates unchanged next week and an 83% probability of a December hike, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.

The US Personal Consumption Expenditures report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, on October 29 could offer further insight.

Elsewhere, gold buying picked up in India this week as lower prices during the major Dussehra festival boosted purchases and lifted premiums, while physical demand in top consumer China was steady even as cautious consumers continued to curb jewellery spending.

Among other metals, spot silver slid 1.3% to $53.81 per ounce, and palladium dropped 0.4% to $1,050.50, hitting their lowest since November 2025 and June 2025 respectively. Spot platinum fell 0.9% to $1,557.03 per ounce, its lowest since July.

All three metals were headed for weekly declines.

data.title: Exclusive-First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows
data.description:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.

Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US mid-term elections.

Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.

The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.

The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.

Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.

"As far as I'm aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.

The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.

RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTS Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.

It also supplies Central Asia by rail.

Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.

It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port-Said, LSEG data showed.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.

Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia's sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.

Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.

(Reporting by Reuters; editing by Philippa Fletcher and Jason Neely)

data.title: Tougher discipline, and Xi's authority, key at China's Communist Party's fifth plenum
data.description:
BEIJING, Oct 23 (Reuters) - China's ruling Communist Party will gather some 300 of its highest-ranking members next week to discuss tightening discipline among its ranks, a conclave analysts say could be the last major party gathering before its 2027 leadership reshuffle.

Although experts widely expect President Xi Jinping to hold onto the party top job for a fourth term at next year's 21st Party Congress, the upcoming plenary session - known as a plenum - offers him an opportunity to shore up authority, enforce ideological uniformity and cement his imprint on the party that rules the world's second-largest economy.

The officials ⁠will deliberate "issues concerning the sustained advancement of full ​and rigorous party self-governance", the party has said, as Xi steps up an internal discipline campaign he introduced in 2014, two years after ascending to power.

The party's current Central Committee, the ​largest of its top decision-making bodies, will convene in the closed-door meeting in Beijing from Monday to Thursday - the fifth ​since the current cohort was formed in 2022 and therefore known as the fifth plenum.

NECESSARY DISCIPLINE

Millions of people within China's vast bureaucracy have been investigated to varying degrees under Xi's anti-corruption campaign, which has purged hundreds of senior officials and top generals - even the president's one-time allies. 

While critics argue the purges - particularly those targeting the highest ranks of the armed forces - are destabilising and undermine combat readiness, the party has portrayed the campaign as both necessary and regenerative, saying the military must undergo a phoenix-like rebirth and "bathe in flames and be forged anew."

"The growing focus on discipline is not because behaviour is getting worse, but because the stakes are getting higher," said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser on China at London's Tony Blair Institute.

Many of Xi's closest associates are likely to retire in the 2027 reshuffle and "disciplinary campaigns are a way to ensure a new generation with fewer personal ties share his political standards," Osman said.

Despite a thinning leadership body, analysts do not expect major personnel moves or any indication of a potential succession plan at the four-day conclave.

"This plenum is probably less about deciding individual promotions, more about signalling the system-wide changes Xi wants ahead of a competitive 2027 Party Congress," Osman said.

In an article published in the party's flagship Qiushi journal days before the plenum, Xi laid out three priorities: enforcing the party leadership's decisions while ensuring uncontested authority, putting the sometimes vast power wielded by its cadres in "an institutional cage", and sustaining the high-pressure anti-graft campaign, while increasing its "penetrating power," indefinitely.

Xi also criticised "two-faced" opportunistic officials who pay lip service to the party leadership while privately resisting its decisions and undermining its authority, as well as those who seek only short-term gains while jeopardising the country's balanced development.

PURGES TRIM NUMBERS

With probes and purges thinning the Central Committee's ranks, turnout among its members "will most likely be the lowest at any post-Mao plenum, below last October's 168 full and 147 alternate members," said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.

"Three of the 24 Politburo members elected in 2022 are gone, the most removed from a sitting Politburo in one term since 1980" as well as five out of the original seven members of the country's supreme military command body, the Central Military Commission, said Mittelstaedt.

The New York-based Asia Society Policy Institute estimates only 77.4% of the original 2022 cohort would be in a position to attend next week's proceedings, meaning nearly a quarter of the leadership body has been removed in the party's disciplinary drive.

The conclave is set to ratify the expulsions of two members of the elite Politburo, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui, over charges including corruption and disloyalty.

(Reporting by Beijing newsroom; Editing by Liz Lee and Lincoln Feast.)
